title: YIMBYs already have a bold vision for solving the housing crisis
gist: Yglesias defends YIMBY land-use deregulation as a radical, expansive agenda — not a narrow one — arguing it would largely solve the country's biggest economic problem, that the postwar public-housing era relied on a far laxer regulatory landscape that no longer exists, and that calling housing 'infrastructure' or spending more on social housing does not substitute for legalizing construction.

insights.claim: The core YIMBY principle — that an owner of land zoned for development should be allowed to build housing on it subject only to bona fide safety and environmental regulation — is radical because it exists nowhere in the United States, not even Houston.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Sets a benchmark showing how far every U.S. jurisdiction is from as-of-right building, implying enormous latent supply that regulation currently suppresses.
insights.quote: There is literally nowhere in the United States of America (no, not even Houston) where it works like that.
insights.locator: But if you asked me what YIMBYism is

insights.claim: Because the status quo is so far from as-of-right building, most concrete YIMBY work is incremental — rolling back staircase requirements, legalizing accessory dwelling units, liberalizing manufactured housing, fourplex bills, parking reform, and transit-oriented upzoning.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Maps the practical policy surface where housing-supply gains actually accrue, useful for tracking which reforms move construction pipelines.
insights.locator: the vast majority of concrete YIMBY work focuses on incremental steps

insights.claim: The circle of intellectuals explicitly arguing against the YIMBY agenda keeps shrinking, and it is now rare to see anyone claim there is no downside to banning new housing where demand is high.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Signals the intellectual argument is largely won even as the local politics remain hard — the remaining fight is over veto rights, not analysis.
insights.locator: the circle of opponents who explicitly argue against the YIMBY agenda keeps shrinking

insights.claim: Leftist intellectuals are reluctant to admit that liberalizing land-use reform would largely solve the country's single biggest economic problem, because conceding that undercuts the larger project of overthrowing 'neoliberalism' for a post-liberal economic order.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Explains the anti-abundance intellectual current as ideologically motivated, predicting continued resistance even where the empirics favor deregulation.
insights.quote: that calls into question the larger project of overthrowing “neo”-liberalism and replacing it with a new post-liberal economic order
insights.locator: But there is a deep reluctance

insights.claim: Christopher Serkin and Daniel Sharfstein dismiss local-regulation arguments as evidence of 'how narrow our imagination has become' and instead propose a mass program of federally financed housing construction.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Names the specific 'abundance is narrow' argument Yglesias rebuts; a marker of the intra-left housing debate shaping Democratic policy direction.
insights.quote: how narrow our imagination has become
insights.locator: This line of thinking is how you get takes like this one

insights.claim: The postwar public-housing boom that anti-abundance writers want to revive took place before the modern regulatory landscape existed — zoning was far laxer, fire codes less strict, and NEPA did not exist.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Undercuts the nostalgia argument: you cannot recreate mid-century construction volumes without also restoring the permissive rules that enabled them.
insights.quote: Zoning was much laxer back then. Fire codes were less strict. NEPA didn’t exist.
insights.locator: The regulatory landscape was different in the past

insights.claim: Los Angeles cut its zoned capacity by 60 percent between 1960 and 1990, and New York City did a massive downzoning in 1961 and was still downzoning on net as recently as the Bloomberg administration.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Hard numbers showing supply capacity was deliberately removed over decades, quantifying the regulatory drag on major-metro housing stock.
insights.quote: Los Angeles cut its zoned capacity by 60 percent between 1960 and 1990.
insights.locator: The regulatory landscape was different in the past

insights.claim: The National Zoning Atlas finds 56 percent of existing single-family-home land is zoned to require lots of at least 40,000 square feet, while just 4 percent allows lots under 10,000 square feet — versus original Levittown lots of 6,000 square feet.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Quantifies how large-lot mandates now foreclose even mid-century-style suburban density, sizing the deregulatory upside.
insights.quote: The National Zoning Atlas finds that 56 percent of existing single-family-home land is zoned to require lots of at least 40,000 square feet.

insights.claim: Harvey Molotch's 1976 'The City as a Growth Machine' described a pro-growth municipal coalition of real-estate, construction, labor, and downtown business interests that was then repeatedly defeated by an explicit 'growth control' movement across the Pacific Coast and Northeast in the 1970s and 1980s.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Provides the historical mechanism by which growth-friendly politics were overturned, framing anti-growth zoning as a reversible political choice.
insights.locator: In 1976, Harvey Molotch published his groundbreaking article

insights.claim: Calling housing 'infrastructure' does not address the real problem, because housing is nothing like a commodity — unlike cars, which are heavily regulated yet freely purchasable, you cannot add dwellings to your lot without neighbors' approval.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Reframes the debate: the binding constraint is the neighbor-veto permission structure, not whether housing is labeled a commodity or infrastructure.
insights.quote: You don’t need to ask your neighbors if they think your car fits with the general vibe of the neighborhood.
insights.locator: Calling things “infrastructure” doesn’t solve the problem

insights.claim: Housing has if anything been treated too much like infrastructure — as a necessary evil communities need to be protected against rather than a commodity people are free to produce.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Inverts the pro-public-housing framing, arguing the problem is protectionist gatekeeping of new supply, not commodification.
insights.quote: treating the mere existence of new homes as a kind of necessary evil that communities need to be protected against
insights.locator: If anything, housing has been treated too much like infrastructure

insights.claim: The U.S. already spends meaningful money on social housing through nonprofit affordable-housing developers, a federal tax credit, and state and city production funds — while simultaneously making it illegal to build on most parcels of land.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Shows the binding constraint is legality of construction, not absence of subsidy, so more social-housing spending without legalization has limited effect.
insights.quote: America already spends meaningful money on social housing — Americans just also make it illegal to build on most parcels of land
insights.locator: the United States has lots of nonprofit affordable-housing developers

insights.claim: Even a high-end estimate of the U.S. housing shortage implies only about a 10 percent expansion of the national housing stock, much of it ADUs and infill rather than large buildings — so broad liberalization need not turn typical neighborhoods into Manhattan.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Bounds the change deregulation would actually produce, a reassurance argument aimed at suburban homeowners wary of dramatic transformation.
insights.quote: we’re probably talking about a 10 percent expansion of the national housing stock

insights.claim: Even with all regulatory barriers removed, housing-stock expansion would remain capped by finite skilled labor and construction equipment, so land-use reform reaches a better equilibrium over time rather than transforming communities overnight.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Flags a skilled-labor bottleneck as the real pacing constraint post-deregulation — relevant to construction-labor demand and trades wages.
insights.quote: there would still be finite amounts of skilled labor and construction equipment
insights.locator: There are also a lot of non-policy limits

insights.claim: Housing is the largest sector of the economy and the number one source of youth economic pessimism, and undue construction barriers are a major blockage of economic growth.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Sizes the stakes: land-use reform is a macro growth lever, not a niche urbanist issue — reason to treat zoning as a first-order economic-policy variable.
insights.quote: Housing is, objectively, the largest sector of the economy and the number one source of youth economic pessimism.
insights.locator: My main issue with this is that it’s not true

insights.claim: Housing abundance would create blue-collar male job opportunities via the skilled-labor bottleneck and make it easier for people to have kids without curbing women's rights or autonomy.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Links deregulation to labor-demand and fertility upside, broadening the political coalition case for supply reform.
insights.locator: Unlocking housing abundance would create new job opportunities

insights.claim: Public-housing enthusiasts have no genuine conflict with YIMBYs because land-use reform makes non-market housing easier to execute; their real dispute is with advocates of spending on other causes.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Argues the intra-progressive fight over housing is misdirected, implying a potential coalition rather than a tradeoff between deregulation and public investment.
insights.quote: Our ideas make it easier to execute their ideas.
insights.locator: the public-housing enthusiasts genuinely have no conflict
